content: Cervical dysplasia identified on a Pap smear is referred to as a squamous intraepithelial lesion (SIL). These abnormalities are categorized into three grades: low-grade (LSIL), high-grade (HSIL), and potentially cancerous (malignant). If a Pap smear reveals abnormal cells or cervical dysplasia, further diagnostic steps or monitoring are recommended. For mild cases, follow-up Pap smears may suffice. In other cases, a colposcopy-directed biopsy can confirm the diagnosis, and a cone biopsy may be performed if necessary after colposcopy. When dysplasia is detected on a cervical biopsy, it is termed cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). CIN is classified into three categories: CIN I (mild dysplasia), CIN II (moderate to marked dysplasia), and CIN III (severe dysplasia to carcinoma in situ). Certain strains of human papillomavirus (HPV) are known to cause cervical cancer. An HPV DNA test can identify high-risk HPV types associated with cervical cancer. This test may be used as a screening tool for women over 30 or for women of any age with slightly abnormal Pap test results. Microinvasive cervical cancer (stage IA) is typically treated with a hysterectomy, which involves the removal of the uterus and part of the vagina. For stage IA2, lymph nodes are also removed. For patients wishing to preserve fertility, local surgical procedures such as a loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) or cone biopsy may be considered. If a cone biopsy does not yield clear margins, a trachelectomy may be an option for patients desiring fertility preservation. This procedure aims to remove the cancer while preserving the ovaries and uterus, offering a more conservative alternative to hysterectomy. Trachelectomy is suitable for stage I cervical cancer that has not spread, but it is not yet a standard treatment due to the limited number of surgeons skilled in this procedure. Even experienced surgeons cannot guarantee the feasibility of a trachelectomy until after microscopic examination during surgery. If clear margins cannot be confirmed, a hysterectomy may still be required, provided the patient has given prior consent. Additionally, lymph node removal may be necessary for pathological evaluation in cases of stage IB or some stage IA cancers due to the risk of cancer spread. A radical trachelectomy can be performed either abdominally or vaginally, with differing opinions on which approach is superior. Radical abdominal trachelectomy with lymphadenectomy typically requires a short hospital stay of two to three days, and most women recover within approximately six weeks. Complications are uncommon, but women who conceive after surgery are at risk for preterm labor and late miscarriage. It is generally advised to wait at least one year before attempting pregnancy after surgery. Recurrence in the residual cervix is rare if the cancer has been cleared, but vigilant follow-up care, including Pap screenings, colposcopy, and biopsies of the remaining lower uterine segment, is recommended every three to four months for at least five years. Patients should also minimize new HPV exposures through safe sex practices until actively trying to conceive. Early-stage cervical cancer (IB1 and IIA less than 4 cm) can be treated with radical hysterectomy and lymph node removal or radiation therapy. Radiation therapy involves external beam radiotherapy to the pelvis and brachytherapy (internal radiation). Patients treated surgically who exhibit high-risk features on pathological examination may receive radiation therapy with or without chemotherapy to reduce the risk of relapse. For larger early-stage tumors (IB2 and IIA greater than 4 cm), treatment options include radiation therapy combined with cisplatin-based chemotherapy, hysterectomy followed by adjuvant radiation therapy, or cisplatin chemotherapy followed by hysterectomy. Advanced-stage tumors (IIB–IVA) are treated with radiation therapy and cisplatin-based chemotherapy. For late-stage cervical cancer (IVB), the FDA has approved a combination of two chemotherapy drugs, Hycamtin (topotecan) and cisplatin, though this combination carries significant risks of neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Invasive cervical carcinoma is considered a relative contraindication to the use of oxytocin. According to the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics, survival improves when radiotherapy is combined with cisplatin-based chemotherapy. As cervical cancer metastasizes to other parts of the body, prognosis worsens significantly because localized treatments are generally more effective than systemic therapies like chemotherapy. Regular screening has enabled the early detection and treatment of precancerous changes and early-stage cervical cancers, saving approximately 5,000 lives annually in the UK. Interval evaluations after therapy are crucial. Recurrent cervical cancer detected early may be treated successfully with surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or a combination of these modalities. In general or low-risk populations, most Pap smear results are normal. In the United States, approximately 2–3 million abnormal Pap smear results are reported annually, with most being mildly abnormal, such as ASC-US (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance) or LSIL (low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion), which often indicate HPV infection. While most low-grade cervical dysplasias regress spontaneously without progressing to cervical cancer, they signal the need for increased vigilance. About 8% of results indicate atypical glandular cells of undetermined significance (AGC-NOS). As liquid-based preparations (LBPs) become more common, atypical result rates have increased slightly. Patients undergoing cervical cancer treatment should prioritize self-care, including maintaining a balanced diet and staying as active as possible. Adequate caloric intake and sufficient protein are essential for maintaining strength and energy. However, treatment side effects such as poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, or mouth sores may make eating challenging. Healthcare providers, including doctors and registered dietitians, can offer strategies to manage these issues. Research indicates that staying active through activities like walking, yoga, or swimming can improve strength, reduce nausea and pain, and alleviate stress. Patients should consult their doctor before starting any physical activity. Regular checkups after cervical cancer treatment are essential to monitor for recurrence and address any health changes. Even when cancer appears to have been completely removed or destroyed, undetected cancer cells may remain in the body, leading to recurrence. Checkups may include physical exams, Pap tests, and chest X-rays. Early detection of recurrent cervical cancer increases the likelihood of successful treatment with surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Teratomas are classified using the Gonzalez-Crussi grading system: grade 0 (mature, benign), grade 1 (immature, probably benign), grade 2 (immature, possibly malignant), and grade 3 (frankly malignant). They are also categorized by content: solid teratomas contain only tissues, cystic teratomas contain fluid or semi-fluid pockets, and mixed teratomas have both solid and cystic components. Cystic teratomas are usually grade 0, and grade 0 teratomas are typically cystic. Grades 0, 1, and 2 pure teratomas have the potential to become malignant (grade 3), and malignant pure teratomas may metastasize. Rare teratomas with malignant transformation (TMT) may contain somatic malignancies such as leukemia, carcinoma, or sarcoma. In infants and young children, these elements are often endodermal sinus tumors or choriocarcinomas. A benign grade 0 teratoma carries a non-zero risk of malignancy. Recurrence with malignant endodermal sinus tumors has been reported in cases of previously benign mature teratomas. Teratomas with malignant transformation (TMT) are rare and may contain somatic malignant elements. Of 641 children with pure teratomas, 9 developed TMT, including carcinoma, glioma, and embryonal tumors. Extraspinal ependymomas, typically considered gliomas, may represent an unusual form of mature teratoma.
